q-76610.name: Question 1
q-76610.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
q-76610.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2−2y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π/2sin2⁡θ(1−3sin2⁡θ)dθ
b
∫0π/22sin3⁡θdθ
c
 ∫0π/2sin2⁡θ(1−cos2⁡θ)dθ
d
∫0π/2sin⁡θ(1−sin⁡θ)dθ
e

EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

x=rcos⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=sin2⁡θ.

q-76673.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-76673.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-76694.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$
q-76694.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the integral of the function f(x,y)=xey+1 along the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π2.

a
2e(e2+1)
b
e2−1
c
2e(e2−1)
d
2(e2−1)
e
2(e2+1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=2cos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π2.

Now, since f(x,y)=xey+1, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θe2sin⁡θ+1.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=22+02=2.

We can now write the integral as

∫Cxey+1ds=∫0π/2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/22cos⁡θe2sin⁡θ+1⋅2⋅dθ=2∫0π/22cos⁡θe2sin⁡θ+1dθ.

We can solve this using the substitution u=2sin⁡θ+1, du=2cos⁡θdθ as follows:

2∫0π/22cos⁡θe2sin⁡θ+1dθ=2∫13eudu=2eu|13=2e3−2e=2e(e2−1)

q-123510.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-123510.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =16{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{u}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
